catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-1-q1.explanation: D - fragmentationFragmentation here means absence of any link between members of society. This is an unusually difficult question, more apt for a CPE exam.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-1-q2.explanation: B - optOpt is the only verb here that collocated with ‘for’ preposition. To opt for means to choose preference for something.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-1-q3.explanation: A - affordAgain, the only verb that collocates well with the immediate context.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-1-q4.explanation: C - take part inThe idea of the sentence is that single people want to get involved in various social activities.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-1-q5.explanation: B - factorFactor is what influences their choice to be alone.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-1-q6.explanation: A - markA mark of success is an accepted collocation.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-1-q7.explanation: C - investThe only verb here that can be used with ‘in’ preposition.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-1-q8.explanation: B - promoteThe idea of the sentence is how individuals of any society help its development. To promote an economic growth is to help the society prosper financially.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-2-q9.explanation: isIt is clear that we need an auxiliary verb here.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-2-q10.explanation: whatWhat if presents a hypothetical (not real) situation.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-2-q11.explanation: less/otherBoth words are acceptable here. Devalued means having its importance lowered or taken away completely.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-2-q12.explanation: insteadOne action taking place instead of another one.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-2-q13.explanation: payTo pay attention is to follow something, to be observant.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-2-q14.explanation: takenTake matters into your hands is to take initiative.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-2-q15.explanation: byThe means of solving the problem is mentioned.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-3-q17.explanation: unresponsiveUsed in conjunction with silent it supposed to have a similar negative meaning. Pay attention to use the right negative suffix.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-3-q18.explanation: contributionsIt is important to use plural form as no certain contribution is implied.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-3-q19.explanation: fabricationsA fabrication is a fake, a made-up thing. This time we should use the plural form, as there is a plural auxiliary verb ‘are’ before the word.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-3-q21.explanation: unappealingThe negative prefix is used because the previous part of the text talks of the phenomenon of fake followers as something bad. However, some people can benefit from this practice because it can boost their popularity. So normally they would find it ‘unappealing’, but for the sake of success they choose NOT to see it as unappealing. A double negative construction is used.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-3-q22.explanation: desirableBe attentive not to spell it wrong. Wrong spelling is counted as incorrect answer.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-3-q23.explanation: illegalMake sure to use the right prefix.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-3-q24.explanation: unethicalSame as before, spelling is crucial.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-4-q25.explanation: have been living here forThe person still lives there so PPC is used.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-4-q26.explanation: no room for anything elseThe word ‘room’ is used in the meaning of ‘free space’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-4-q27.explanation: before have I seenInversion is used here for more dramatic effect.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-4-q28.explanation: was dismissive ofTo be dismissive means to be unwilling to accept something, in this case — not wanting to accept or even consider the idea offered to her.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-4-q29.explanation: no circumstances must/can/should youAnother case of inversion for a more emphatic effect.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-4-q30.explanation: I take your pointTo take one’s point is to understand why a person thinks or does so.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-5-q31.explanation: BThe answer is in the middle of the third sentence, paragraph one: people doubt how they could use the information they got from those motivational speeches.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-5-q32.explanation: AThe first sentence of paragraph two states that we need to find out the reason why some people try their best and others don’t. Simply put — the factors that affect motivation.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-5-q33.explanation: CLast sentence of paragraph four contains the answer. It isn’t an obvious one, but after you rule out the rest of answers, it remains to be the only one. Answer A is wrong — it is clearly stated that the successful people have to work harder that others. Nothing is said about talent playing a role in becoming successful. Answer D isn’t correct — all people learn at ‘identical rates’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-5-q34.explanation: CThe author wants to reinforce the point by posing natural questions — why would people put effort if it doesn’t change anything. A talented person is going to be successful in any case, and one without a talent will lose no matter what.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-5-q35.explanation: AEmployees need to be encouraged in order to have their ambition reinforced. This is where their employer is advised to show the fruits of hard labour, to indicate the career pathway to the top.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-5-q36.explanation: AIt is important to understand ‘yank-and-rank’, because the meaning isn’t clear from the context. It is a system where a company ranks every employee against others and terminates the contracts of those who seem worse in comparison. In the text, it says that this system makes the lower-ranking staff seem unable to learn, which is wrong. Thus, there is lack of attention to personal development of employees.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-6-q37.explanation: DReviewer A believes that a baby’s mind is well capable of analysing the happenings of everyday life, not simply ‘live through them’. Reviewer D doubts children’s ability to interpret and analyse the world: “she sometimes seems to go too far, as when claiming that babies recognise the actions they copy and reproduce”.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-6-q38.explanation: CBoth Reviewers C and D talks about something that parent have known for a long time - Text C: “…this is something most parents of teenagers are well aware of.“; Text D: “…she is spending too much time simply confirming what parents and preschool teachers have long known.“

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-6-q39.explanation: DReviewer B believes that a child’s brain is similar to a scientist experimenting with data. Reviewer D agrees: “they are creative and innovative, though not always correct”.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-6-q40.explanation: CAt the end of Reviewer’s C text they suggest :”… she provides insights into the human mind in general.” This implies that the author has covered general points, but wasn’t ‘comprehensive enough’ — not explaining everything in full detail.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-7-q41.explanation: DThe beginning of D starts with patients making “such claims” (mentioned at the very end of previous paragraph) all the time, and if granted a leave, they are likely to cause trouble. At the end of Paragraph D the author poses a question. The following paragraph continues the idea — it makes Ekman think of the question.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-7-q42.explanation: AThe previous paragraph ends with Ekman going through a recording, trying to find a hidden expression on patient’s face. Paragraph A talks about three more cases he managed to find while browsing the recording.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-7-q43.explanation: G“Seven basic emotions” mentioned in the previous paragraph are the beginning and the main idea of this paragraph. At the end of the paragraph it is suggested that these emotions can be hidden, but next paragraph says that it is very difficult to achieve.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-7-q44.explanation: BThe last question of this paragraph helps us to connect it to the next one. The way to apply these techniques to crime-solving is mentioned in the next paragraph.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-7-q45.explanation: FAn easy question here, as the paragraph before clearly states that there is going to be an example next. This paragraph illustrates a hypothetical situation of using the technique to see through a person’s lie.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-7-q46.explanation: CThis and the next paragraph concentrate on the minor details that help to understand what really is on person’s mind.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-8-q47.explanation: CMiddle of the paragraph: “… you’ll welcome movies that pay attention to characterisation and dialogue…“.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-8-q48.explanation: DSecond sentence of Paragraph D goes on about the importance of a feel-good movie during a less fortunate period of human history.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-8-q49.explanation: BThe movie’s character “revises his own priorities” after going through a difficult period of their life.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-8-q50.explanation: BLast sentence of the paragraph explains what made author make the movie and what message he decided to carry across — “leave preaching to the preachers”.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-8-q51.explanation: A It is stated in the middle of the paragraph how cinema becomes a recognised form of art, just like music, theatre, painting and the rest.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-8-q52.explanation: BEscapism is the desire to escape from harsh reality. Second part of the sentence mentions the importance of it in the example with cartoons.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-8-q53.explanation: AThe technique of cross-cutting was used that made the narrative more dramatic and the culmination — more satisfying.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-8-q54.explanation: CSecond part of the paragraph states that a feel-good movie doesn’t have to ‘be dumb’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-8-q55.explanation: BThis is a tricky one — it is about the example with Battleship Potemkin. The author hints at the idea, without saying it outright — when you are in a tough situation, you start worrying about the basics and not something exquisite.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test7-part-8-q56.explanation: DMiddle of the paragraph mentions how a group of characters manages to win the struggle with ‘big, bad, interfering bureaucrats‘.
